glossary.meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will," and "assists, protects, and defends it." Which one began the good, grace or the will, we left open. We held grace together with a free will on purpose - in a relation "that cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man."

At Tours, virtus is not first a moral quality but effective power. It is the "power present" Martin feels before he raises the dead, and the "abundance of power" he had as a monk and had less of as a bishop. At Marseilles Cassian uses the same word for moral virtue, and declines on principle to "weave a tale of God's miracles and signs."

In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders.

The picture that governed a monk's life among us. A man had changed service - from Caesar's army, or from a worldly career - to Christ's. He now stood girded, under oath, in daily combat against the devil and his own faults. The one who slackened was, in Cassian's word, a deserter.
Vincent's book. By its own name it is an aid to memory, against his own forgetting. He signs it "Peregrinus, the least of all the servants of God" - a teller, not an author.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Vincent, presbyter of the island, who wrote as Peregrinus
pull_quotes.text: In God there is one substance but three Persons. In Christ there are two substances but one Person.

The Lord Jesus never said he would come back dressed in purple, with a glittering crown on his head. I will not believe Christ has come unless he comes looking the way he did when he suffered, and openly shows the marks of his wounds from the cross.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: one of the elders of Egypt, unnamed, as Cassian reports him (Institutes V.24)
pull_quotes.text: I can fast any day. But I am about to walk you on your way, and I will not have you with me for long. A fast is good and worth doing, but it is a gift I choose to give. Charity is a command, and a command has to be carried out. So since I receive Christ in you, I ought to feed him. Once I have sent you on, I can make up for the welcome I gave for his sake by fasting more strictly on my own. For "the bridegroom's friends cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them." But once he has gone, then they will rightly fast.

cite.text: The monks and clergy of Marseilles and Lerins were "the Massilians" - "the remnants of the Pelagians," the semi-Pelagian party - a school of one doctrine, opposed to predestination, that Cassian, Vincent, and Faustus alike held and that Rome condemned.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Did you believe people are saved by faith alone, not works?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Neither half of that is the shape our own life gave the question. Hear it as a brother heard it. Among the brethren at Marseilles a monk fasts, watches, keeps his cell, and lays every thought bare to the senior. At the moment he feels the fast has done something, he is taught to say that it was not he, but the grace of God with him. Both halves are commanded. Cassian set it down as the elders' teaching, not his own: perfection cannot be gained without these labours, and by these labours alone, without the grace of God, no one can attain it. The will always remains free in a man; and it is weak; and the help of God is needed by it every day and hour. The argument came to us as a story. Two friends came back to morning service in Egypt troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before - that a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder saw them whispering, cut the psalms short, and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. He cannot ascribe the crop to himself. And God does not send rich crops to the idle. That morning the elder drew one conclusion. The start even of our good thoughts comes from God, who first stirs a good will in us. Our part is to follow, humbly, day by day, the grace that draws us. Later in the same teaching he put it the other way as well. Two things we refused. We refused the notion that gives everything to the will and hands out grace by a man's deserts; Vincent, on the island, named Pelagius for it. And we refused, as grievous blasphemy, the thought that God does not will all men to be saved. How both are true - how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. If you ask which side we stood on, our teacher would not answer that with a formula. He kept both sides in one sentence.

cite.text: To stop tribunes from hunting heretics in the Spains, Martin takes communion once with the bishops he had refused. An angel tells him his remorse is just. He feels his power lessened, and he never attends a synod again.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Your church used power against Christians who disagreed. Defend that.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Our own saint did not defend it, and he was there. This is what happened. A synod of bishops had condemned a man and his followers as heretics in their absence, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court at Treves. The accuser there was himself a bishop, and the bishops gathered in the city were daily in communion with him and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that the bishops had done enough when they declared men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, Sulpitius says, to protect even heretics themselves. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion failed, the emperor grew angry, and executioners were named for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall. He left the city in grief, sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and afterward, when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again. So the sword was drawn in the Church's cause among us, by bishops. The man we remember is the one who yielded once to stop it, and grieved over it afterward. We do not defend it, and the man at the centre of it never called it right. Two limits belong with it. The accuser is heard only through the man who called him worthless. And on the island Vincent, in his own voice, held that one who preaches other than what was received is to be cut off, lest one sick sheep infect the flock. He looked to an ancient council as the guard of the faith. Our two houses never argued any of this with each other.

cite.text: Purity of heart as the goal, discretion as its regulator, the eight faults as its combats - what Cassian wrote out for the monks of Gaul from the Fathers: 'the immediate aim or goal, is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end' (Conf. I.4); fastings, vigils, and renunciation 'are not perfection, but aids to perfection' (I.7); 'discretion is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator' (II.4); the eight faults 'and the remedies for them according to their traditions' (Inst. Pref.); vainglory that 'creates a wish to take holy orders' (Inst. XI.14). In Tours, the thing appears without the vocabulary. Martin sees through Anatolius's robe and the purple-robed 'Christ' (Vita XXIII-XXIV). But there is no talk of purity of heart, no discretion, no list of faults. Cassian frames every element of this program as received from Egypt, not his own invention; what Gaul contributed was the adaptation - carried west and adapted for a colder climate (Inst. I.10, IV.10-11), its severity sustained by a real fear of spiritual cooling. The English edition this account draws on leaves out two of Cassian's conferences on this program: XII, on chastity, and XXII, on nocturnal illusions. It also leaves out Institutes VI.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your way of life offer someone who struggled to quiet their own mind?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: A mill that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. And a lesson taught early: every itching thought was laid bare to the senior as soon as it rose, before it was acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The fathers knew the hour the mind revolts, too. About the sixth hour a monk comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, goes in and out, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. They called it accidie, and their remedy was to stay. All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

cite.text: A citizen lures a monk out of his monastery by pretending his wife is ill. The monk is taken to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops object to his mean clothes and his hair. A psalm read at random answers them.

The monk-bishop came to office as a captive, never as a candidate. Martin was drawn from his monastery by a trick and made bishop of Tours by the one wish of all the people, over the impious resistance of a few bishops whose only objection was that his clothing was mean and his hair disgusting, and the objectors were confounded by a psalm; the same shape holds at every house - Honoratus overtaken by the dignity he fled, Archebius "carried off" - so that nobody in this world's own stories wanted the see.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who chose your leaders — were bishops appointed, elected, or something else?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Something else. Among us the office was not sought; it came for the man who had fled it. This is how it came at Tours. Martin could not easily be drawn out of his monastery, so a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at his knees and pretended his wife was ill. Crowds had been posted along the road, and he was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people of Tours and the neighbouring cities had one wish, that Martin was the worthiest man for the episcopate. A few of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, and his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the office came to its founder when he was made a presbyter: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. No house wrote of another's. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and given to a town as its bishop, and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it. Our own teaching made wanting the office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride. So no one in our stories wanted the see. Hear the limit of that. Every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder. Sulpitius was not present at the election, and he was no friend to the bishops who objected. Those bishops left no account; what their case was beyond clothes and hair, no one kept. Whether every reluctance was as whole as our stories say, the men who could have contradicted them never wrote.

quiet.statement: If you dug up the places we lived, we could not tell you what you would find. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's Institutes, written for a bishop's new house, and his book of the elders' talks; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us. Even the names you may know for our places are not in our own books, so we do not use them. What we can tell you of daily life comes from what Cassian said Egypt did. It also comes from his complaint that no one in Gaul kept it up unbroken even a year, and from what Sulpitius said the saint did in his cell. Of the island's own day, not a line. What we ate, where we slept, what the rooms looked like - only as far as those pages say, and no further.

dates.display: d. 397, on a peacemaking journey to Condate; a soldier under 'Julian Caesar' in his youth, discharged at a donative; monk 'not far from the town' where Hilary was bishop, then bishop of Tours from an undated election (the monastery across the river founded 'after 371' only on the editorial introduction's word); 'lived sixteen years' after the Treves affair by Gallus's own reckoning

writing c. 397 (the Life; Letter III within months of Martin's death) to c. 404-406 (the Dialogues); an Aquitanian 'of an illustrious family' who visited Martin at Tours; birth and death years rest only on the modern editors' disagreeing endnotes and are not asserted

travelled in Egypt with Germanus in his youth (the interval to his writing not stated in this world's own documents); founded the twin houses at Marseilles c. 415; wrote the Institutes for Castor before 426 and the Conferences in three parts, Part II (to Honoratus and Eucherius) not later than 426; d. c. 435

names.name: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

dates.display: founded the community on the island of Lerins c. 400-410 (410 on the surviving volume's editorial introduction); addressed by Cassian as a brother presiding over a large monastery, then as a bishop - the see identified as Arles, from 426, only by the editorial apparatus; d. c. 429/430, the year his disciple and successor Hilary preached his life

names.name: Honoratus, the founder of the island
Honoratus of Lerins, later bishop of Arles (d. c. 429/430)

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Martin was the soldier who left the army for Christ. He was made a bishop against his own will. Sulpitius Severus was the admirer who wrote almost everything we know about him. He admits he was never present for it himself. Cassian lived among Egypt's monks and carried their teaching to Marseilles. He refused to write of wonders. Honoratus founded a community on an island of snakes. Like Martin, he was overtaken by an office he never sought.

documented_stories.teaser: A soldier cuts his cloak in two for a naked beggar at the city gate. That night he sees Christ wearing the half he gave away.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A catechumen soldier has nothing left but his cloak. He cuts it in two for a naked beggar at a city gate. That night he sees Christ wearing the half he gave away.
documented_stories.telling:
Sulpitius tells us how Martin began, before any monastery existed in Gaul. The son of a military tribune, an army officer, Martin was seized at fifteen on his father's information and forced to take the soldier's oath. Even then he kept only one servant, and served that servant himself. He was still a catechumen, preparing for baptism, and kept from his pay only what each day required.

One unusually harsh winter was proving fatal to many from the cold. At the gate of the city of Amiens, Martin met a poor man with no clothes, whom everyone else passed by. Martin had nothing left but his weapons and his cloak. He drew his sword, cut the cloak into two equal halves, and gave one to the poor man. Some bystanders laughed at him, while others felt ashamed, since they had more than Martin and had never done anything like it.

That night, the account says, Martin saw Christ in his sleep, wearing the half he had given away. Christ told the surrounding angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Sulpitius says Martin did not grow proud, and he went and was baptized at twenty. His tribune had promised to leave the world with him, so he served almost two more years, a soldier in name only.

Sulpitius witnessed none of this, and learned it partly from Martin and partly from those who had lived with him. The text provides no year and never names the beggar.
documented_stories.title: Half a Cloak at the Gate of Amiens
documented_stories.when: While Martin was still a soldier and not yet baptized; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: Called a coward for refusing to fight, a soldier offers to walk at the enemy with no weapons. Before morning, the enemy asks for peace.
documented_stories.tellable_as: At a donative before a battle, a soldier tells Caesar he is now the soldier of Christ and may not fight. He offers to stand unarmed before the enemy. The next day the enemy asks for peace.
documented_stories.telling:
Sulpitius tells us, in his Life of Martin, how Martin left the army. Barbarian raiders were pushing into Gaul, and Julian Caesar gathered an army at a place the text calls the city of the Vaugiones. There he began giving out a donative, a gift of money, calling his soldiers forward one by one. When Martin's turn came, he decided this was the moment to request his discharge, refusing the money since he did not mean to stay.

He told Caesar that he had served him as a soldier long enough, and now he asked to become a soldier to God. As the soldier of Christ, he said, it was not lawful for him to fight. Julian, whom Sulpitius calls the tyrant, accused him of cowardice and of running from the coming battle. The charge only made Martin more determined. He offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line the next day, protected by nothing except the sign of the cross.

He was returned to prison to await the morning. On the following day the enemy sent messengers to ask for peace, surrendering themselves and everything they had, so no battle was fought. Sulpitius asks who could doubt that this victory was due to the saintly man. He reads it as God sparing Martin the sight of others dying.

That interpretation belongs to Sulpitius himself. He was not present, the text gives no year, and no independent witness survives.
documented_stories.title: Martin Asks Caesar for His Discharge
documented_stories.when: c. 360, before a battle in Gaul, on the eve of Martin's discharge from the Roman army

documented_stories.teaser: Martin returns to find a new believer dead before baptism. He bolts the door and stretches himself over the body. Two hours later the man opens his eyes.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Martin returns to find a catechumen dead and unbaptized. He bolts the door and stretches himself on the body. He perceives that power is present, and two hours later the man opens his eyes. Afterward the man tells of the tribunal and the two angels that sent him back.
documented_stories.telling:
Sulpitius tells us about the first of Martin's works of power, the miracle that made his name famous. Martin had founded a monastery for himself not far from the town. A catechumen, a man still preparing for baptism, joined him there, wanting to be formed by his teaching and example. Within a few days the man developed a fever. While Martin was away for three days, the man died so suddenly that he was never baptized.

As the account tells it, Martin sent everyone out of the cell, bolted the door, and stretched himself full length on the body. He prayed until he sensed that power was present, and then he waited for the Lord's mercy. Scarcely two hours passed before the dead man began to stir and opened his eyes. Martin cried out his thanks so loudly that the brothers rushed in and found him alive. The catechumen was baptized at once and lived for many years afterward.

The man himself used to describe his experience. He was brought before the Judge and assigned to gloomy places among common crowds. Then two angels declared that this was the man for whom Martin was praying, and they returned him to Martin. From that day, Sulpitius says, people considered Martin holy, powerful, and truly apostolic.

Sulpitius presents the man as a living witness, yet never names him. He identifies the monastery only as a place not far from the town.
documented_stories.title: Martin Brings a Dead Catechumen Back
documented_stories.when: After Martin left the army and set up his monastery; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: A citizen feigns a sick wife to draw a monk from his monastery. Some bishops object to his shabby clothes and hair. A psalm opened at random answers them.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A citizen lures a monk out of his monastery by pretending his wife is ill. The monk is taken to the city under a kind of guard. Some bishops object to his mean clothes and his hair. A psalm read at random answers them.
documented_stories.telling:
Sulpitius tells us how Martin, a monk, became bishop of Tours. Martin could not easily be drawn out of his monastery. So a citizen named Ruricius pretended that his wife was sick, and he knelt before Martin, begging him to come. Once Martin came out, citizens lining the road escorted him into the city as though he were under guard. An enormous crowd from Tours and the neighboring towns had gathered to vote, and nearly everyone agreed that Martin deserved the office.

A few people opposed the choice, including some of the bishops summoned to consecrate him. They called him contemptible, with shabby clothing and disgusting hair, and Defensor, one of the bishops, led the opposition. The crowd only laughed at their objections.

That day the appointed reader could not get through the crowd, and the officials stood confused. Someone nearby picked up the book of psalms and read the first verse he found. It said that God had perfected praise from the mouths of babies and infants, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. The crowd shouted, and Defensor's side fell silent. People believed God had chosen the verse so that Defensor would hear a testimony to his own resistance. As bishop, Sulpitius adds, Martin kept the dignity of his office and the simple habits of a monk.

Sulpitius gives no year for the election. He is openly hostile to the objecting bishops, whose own side is never heard.
documented_stories.title: The Monk Tricked Into the Bishop's Chair
documented_stories.when: Years after Martin's discharge; the text gives no year

documented_stories.teaser: A bishop shares communion with men he had refused, so that troops will not be sent to hunt heretics in Spain. He never fully forgives himself.
documented_stories.tellable_as: To stop tribunes from hunting heretics in the Spains, Martin takes communion once with the bishops he had refused. An angel tells him his remorse is just. He feels his power lessened, and he never attends a synod again.
documented_stories.telling:
Sulpitius tells this in his Dialogues through Gallus, one of Martin's disciples, who says Martin told it only within his household. After Priscillian was put to death, the emperor Maximus shielded Ithacius, the bishop who had accused him. The bishops at Treves, now Trier, backed Ithacius. Maximus was about to send tribunes, army officers, into Spain to hunt heretics and take their lives or goods. Martin begged at court that none be sent, to spare the heretics as well as the true Christians. In his Sacred History, Sulpitius states Martin's view that a worldly ruler judging a church case was a shocking wrong.

The bishops begged Maximus to turn on Martin, and he ordered the deaths of the very people Martin had defended. Martin rushed to the palace at night and promised to take communion with the bishops if those lives were spared. Maximus agreed, and the next day Martin took communion when a bishop named Felix was ordained. Yet the bishops could never get him to sign it.

Leaving the city, Martin was filled with grief and sat alone in the woods near a village called Andethanna. Gallus says an angel told him his remorse was just, though he had had no other way out. Afterward his healing sometimes came more slowly, and with tears he blamed that single communion. He lived sixteen more years and never went to a synod again.

The text gives no year, and we hear Ithacius only through the writer who called him worthless.
documented_stories.title: Martin Yields Once, at the Emperor's Court
documented_stories.when: 385/386, after the execution of Priscillian and his companions at Trier

documented_stories.teaser: A presbyter Martin raised from boyhood rages at him, then begs pardon within the hour. Martin will not remove him. If Christ bore with Judas, why not Brictio?
documented_stories.tellable_as: A presbyter Martin raised from boyhood storms into the courtyard. He calls his master's visions ridiculous fancies, then soon comes back and begs pardon. Martin will not remove him: if Christ bore with Judas, why should he not bear with Brictio?
documented_stories.telling:
In the Dialogues, Sulpitius has Gallus describe one day at Martin's dwelling. Martin was sitting on his wooden seat in the small open court outside his door. Gallus says Martin saw two demons sitting on the rock above the monastery. They called out with joy, "Come here, Brictio, come here, Brictio." Then Brictio rushed in, furious and out of his mind.

The day before, Martin had rebuked him, because Brictio had owned nothing when he entered the clergy and was now buying horses and slaves. Many said the slaves included boys bought from beyond the frontier and girls chosen for their looks. Brictio had been raised in the monastery by Martin himself. Pale with rage, he claimed to be the holier man, since he had grown up in the Church while Martin had been a soldier. He called Martin's visions ridiculous fantasies and nearly struck him, while Martin answered him gently.

Brictio left believing he had won, but he soon returned, threw himself at Martin's feet, and begged for forgiveness. He confessed that a demon had taken hold of him, and Martin forgave him easily. Later, whenever Brictio was accused of serious wrongdoing, Martin refused to remove him from his position as a presbyter, a priest. He did not want anyone to suspect him of avenging his own injury. He bore with Brictio, he said, as Christ had borne with Judas.

Brictio's own side is never heard, since every word of his reaches us through men hostile to him.
documented_stories.title: If Christ Bore with Judas
documented_stories.when: Undated; told in Sulpitius's Dialogues, about 404 to 406

documented_stories.teaser: Knowing his end is near, Martin goes to make peace among quarreling clergy. Dying, he turns down straw for sackcloth and ashes, so as not to set a softer example.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Foreknowing his death, Martin goes to make peace among quarrelling clerics. He sickens, and refuses straw for his bed of sackcloth and ashes rather than set his disciples a softer example. At his funeral, it is said, nearly two thousand monks gather, old men and young soldiers of Christ, with a choir of virgins.
documented_stories.telling:
Sulpitius describes Martin's death in a letter to his mother-in-law, Bassula, admitting he was not present. Martin, he writes, had long known the approaching time of his death. When the clergy at Condate began quarrelling, Martin travelled there to make peace, judging one more church at peace a fitting conclusion to his life.

With peace restored, his strength suddenly failed, and his weeping brothers begged him not to abandon them. Martin prayed that he would not refuse further work if he was still needed, and left the decision to God. For some days he lay feverish on sackcloth and ashes, praying through entire nights. When his disciples asked to put common straw beneath him, he refused, saying a Christian should die among ashes. He would be sinning, he said, if he left them a different example. Witnesses reported that he saw the devil standing nearby and rebuked him fearlessly. He died, and those present testified that his face resembled an angel's.

Sulpitius says the whole city and the surrounding villages poured out to meet the body. At the funeral, almost two thousand monks are said to have gathered, old men and young soldiers of Christ. A choir of virgins also came, concealing their grief.

The letter never names the city where the body was taken, and the numbers are report. The choir of virgins is the only trace of the women who embraced this life at Tours, and none of them speaks.
documented_stories.title: Martin Refuses the Straw

documented_stories.teaser: Egyptian fathers cannot agree how many psalms to sing each evening. The hour for prayer arrives, and one father sings twelve and vanishes. They take twelve as the number.
documented_stories.tellable_as: The fathers of Egypt argue whether the daily psalms should be fifty or sixty. The Vesper hour interrupts them. One father rises to sing, finishes the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanishes. The number is fixed forever, not by any monk but by an angel.
documented_stories.telling:
Cassian passed this story on to Gaul in his Institutes. We received it as the fathers of Egypt telling how their own rule of prayer began. In the earliest days, they say, only a few of the best men were called monks. They lived like the first believers in Jerusalem, of one heart and soul, holding everything in common. The elder fathers met to arrange the daily worship for the generations that would follow them.

Each father considered only his own strength and proposed whatever number of psalms suited him. Some argued for fifty psalms, some for sixty, and some for even more. The disagreement was still unresolved when the hour for evening prayer arrived.

So they paused for worship, and one father rose to chant while the others sat listening attentively. He sang eleven psalms, each followed by its own prayer, and then he finished the twelfth with Alleluia. At that moment he vanished from their sight. The fathers understood this as the work of Providence, a rule fixed for every community through the angel's own act. From then on they kept twelve psalms for the evening and night prayers, adding two readings later by their own choice.

Cassian names no witness who saw the angel, and nothing in our record says what the brothers at Tours sang. In Gaul the twelve were kept, together with a hymn of praise called the Gloria, which Cassian says was never heard in the East.
documented_stories.title: The Angel Who Fixed the Psalms
documented_stories.when: Set in the early days of Egypt's monks, no year given; Cassian wrote it down in Gaul

documented_stories.teaser: Two friends come to morning prayer troubled by one sentence from the night before. The old man cuts the service short and answers with a farmer who still needs rain.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Two friends come back to morning prayer troubled by one sentence an old man added the night before: no one masters the good by his own toil. The old man cuts the office short. He answers with a farmer who still needs the rain.
documented_stories.telling:
At the beginning of his Thirteenth Conference, Cassian describes how the question of grace and effort first arose. It came up in Egypt between two friends at prayer, at an old man's cell near Panephysis. Cassian wrote it down much later in Gaul, for the brothers Honoratus and Eucherius.

He and Germanus had spent the evening listening to the old man Chaeremon teach about chastity. One sentence troubled Germanus, that even striving with all one's might cannot make a person master of the good without receiving it as a gift. After a short sleep they returned for morning prayer, still whispering about it. Chaeremon noticed, shortened the service, and asked what was wrong.

Germanus argued that chastity is won by hard and lasting effort, just as a farmer earns the credit for his harvest. Chaeremon turned the farmer's example back on him. No farmer can claim the harvest by his labor alone, because he depends on rain he cannot control. Yet God gives no rich crop to a farmer who never ploughs. So, Chaeremon concluded, both the desire to do good and the opportunity to do it come from God first. The human part is to follow that grace day by day.

That morning's answer grew into the entire Conference. Later Chaeremon says that grace works together with the human will, and that the human mind cannot fully understand how both are true. What he taught about chastity the night before is missing from our edition.
documented_stories.title: The Farmer Who Still Needs the Rain
documented_stories.when: Set in Egypt, no year given; Cassian wrote it down in Gaul, not later than 426

documented_stories.teaser: A founder walks unafraid onto an island shunned for its snakes, singing a psalm. The snakes give way. Then the priest's headband catches the man who ran from it.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Hilary tells how Honoratus went unafraid onto an island shunned for its filth and its serpents, with a psalm on his lips. The serpents gave way, and a camp of God rose there. There, as far as his sermon can be read, the priest's headband caught the man who had run from it.
documented_stories.telling:
Hilary, the disciple who succeeded Honoratus at Arles, preached his life at his death. This is how our community at Lerins remembers its founder, as far as the rough copy of that sermon can be read.

Honoratus, Hilary says, left his homeland longing for the desert. Near the city lay an island that stood empty because of its excessive squalor, and no one could approach it for fear of venomous creatures. He was drawn there by the opportunity for seclusion, and by the nearness of the holy bishop Leontius, whom he loved. He longed to be cut off from the world, even by the sea. In heart and mouth he carried the psalm about walking on the asp and the basilisk, both serpents, and trampling the lion and the dragon.

So he went in unafraid, Hilary says, and his own calm scattered his companions' fear. The horror of the place fled, and the crowd of serpents gave way. Serpents were often met there, Hilary says, yet they never harmed or even frightened anyone, and he counts this among his master's miracles. Honoratus established a camp of God in that place. There the priesthood overtook the man who had fled it, and he was made a presbyter, a priest, while keeping a monk's humility.

This is the closest our record comes to Lerins itself. It tells how the founder arrived and was made a priest there. What anyone did on the island in between, it does not say.
documented_stories.title: Honoratus and the Island of Snakes
documented_stories.when: Told in a funeral sermon by his successor at Arles; the text gives no year

floor_note.text: This world confessed what the wider Church confessed about Christ. But its own life rarely argued about it. Vincent, writing from the island, gave one formula as an example of a settled faith, not a live debate: one substance but three Persons in God, two substances but one Person in Christ. He wrote it to defend a different point. Mary should be called the mother of God, he said, not only of the man Christ. A council had already ruled on that, three years before he wrote. This world's real argument lay elsewhere: how much of a monk's own progress comes from God's gift, and how much from his own effort. On that question, this world's own record never reaches a settled answer.

legacy.text: This world's own record stops before its central argument was settled. It says so itself: what comes after is not its to tell. One generation later, the argument about grace and effort continued. But it was no longer monks writing to fellow monks. A bishop trained on the same island took it up instead, writing at the direct request of two church councils. This world's own record ends at the edge of that change, not inside it.

read_first.note: The whole of Martin's own story, told by a man who loved him and was never present for any of it.

source.citation: Sulpitius Severus, On the Life of St. Martin (Vita Martini), trans. Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11, ed. Schaff and Wace

read_first.note: Egypt's customs, carried west and adapted for a colder climate and a bishop's new house.

source.citation: John Cassian, The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, trans. Edgar C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11, ed. Schaff and Wace

read_first.note: A short book written as a rule for telling true growth in the faith from a corruption dressed up as one.

source.citation: Vincent of Lerins, The Commonitory, trans. C. A. Heurtley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11, ed. Schaff and Wace

relations_summary.text: This world grew up on ground another community had already fought to hold. Before Martin's own household took shape, a bishop named Hilary of Poitiers was sent into exile. He had refused to accept a creed backed by the emperor. Once he came home, Hilary was the bishop near whom Martin first gathered his own followers. This world's own record does not say what happened to Gaul's church after its own span closes in 450. It says nothing about monasticism elsewhere, either.

sourcing.text: This world's record is richest in one man's telling of another. Sulpitius Severus wrote about Martin. Cassian wrote down what Egypt's monks taught him. Both households left rich writing about ideas and virtues. But both leave two things almost entirely dark: the island's own daily life, and Tours's own daily worship. No one wrote down what the brethren sang, or when. No woman's own word survives from either house, though both kept communities of women alongside the men. And a later editor cut three whole sections on the body's own discipline from the one edition of Cassian that survives. That is a gap in what survives, not in what this world itself said.

story.text: In Roman Gaul, between about 360 and 450 CE, two households of monks lived out one idea. One grew up in the Loire valley, around the town of Tours. The other grew up on an island called Lérins, off the Mediterranean coast, and in the nearby city of Marseilles. Nothing in the evidence shows the two ever wrote to each other. Both called themselves keepers of what came before them.

The northern household began with a soldier named Martin. While he served under Julian, then Caesar, he asked for his discharge before a battle. He would serve Christ now, he said. Years later the people of Tours took him from his monastery by a trick and made him their bishop. As bishop, Martin kept living like a monk outside the city walls. Many monks he trained were later made bishops themselves.

Two generations later, a man named Honoratus went alone to a small island off the coast. Snakes had driven everyone else away. He went in unafraid, singing a psalm, and the record says the snakes gave way. He wanted only to stay a monk there. Even so, he later became bishop of the nearby city of Arles. Faustus, another monk trained on the island, became bishop of Riez.

Both households measured themselves against the monks of Egypt. In the south, that meant reception. Cassian lived among the Egyptian monks and brought their customs home to Gaul, changing only what the colder climate required. In the north, it meant comparison. Sulpitius has a traveler from Egypt say that Martin alone was worth all its hermits put together. Both households also agreed that nothing true could be new. Vincent, a monk on Lérins, wrote that true faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by everyone.

The south named its goal purity of heart. Cassian taught that fasting and night prayer were only aids toward it. What matters most is discretion, which he called the mother of all virtues. Tours built its record on power instead. Martin once brought a dead catechumen, a new believer not yet baptized, back to life. Another night the devil came to him dressed as Christ. Martin refused him. The only Christ he would accept still carried the marks of his wounds. Cassian warned that a monk who boasts of casting out demons has already failed.

The south's best-known argument began as a worry at prayer. In Egypt, Cassian and his friend Germanus heard an elder say that no one becomes master of the good by effort alone. Asked what he meant, he answered with a farmer's field. A farmer who will not plow gets no harvest. But even a hard worker gets nothing without rain he cannot make. The wish to do good, the elder said, starts with God. That answer grew into a long argument over how much of a monk's progress is God's gift and how much is his own. It later reached Rome. The record never settles it.

On bishops and councils, the two households disagreed. At Tours, Martin kept his distance from other bishops. At the emperor's court in Trier, he once took communion with bishops he had refused, to save lives. He regretted it for the rest of his life and never attended a synod again. In the south, church councils were trusted as guardians of the truth. The record leaves that disagreement standing.

Almost everything known about Tours comes from one writer. Sulpitius Severus was a layman who gave up his career to follow Martin. He was never present for the events he describes, and he says so himself. When Martin's death drew near, he traveled to make peace among quarreling clergy. His monks wanted to lay him on straw. He chose sackcloth and ashes, so as not to leave them a different example. Sulpitius says almost two thousand monks gathered for his funeral. The record closes around 450, with the argument over grace and effort still open.

dates.display: d. 397, on a peacemaking journey to Condate; a soldier under 'Julian Caesar' in his youth, discharged at a donative; monk 'not far from the town' where Hilary was bishop, then bishop of Tours from an undated election (the monastery across the river founded 'after 371' only on the editorial introduction's word); 'lived sixteen years' after the Treves affair by Gallus's own reckoning

voices.hedge: Everything told about Martin comes from one writer, Sulpitius Severus, who loved him and was never present for any of it. Sulpitius says so himself. That single-author risk runs through every story this world tells about its own founder.
voices.text: Martin left the army to serve Christ instead, telling his commander it was not right for him to fight. He gathered followers in the woods near Tours, then was made bishop against his own will. As bishop, he never stopped living like a monk. He healed the sick and raised the dead, by his own account, yet felt that power lessen once he took a communion he believed was wrong, just to save two men's lives. He never sat with a group of bishops again.

dates.display: travelled in Egypt with Germanus in his youth (the interval to his writing not stated in this world's own documents); founded the twin houses at Marseilles c. 415; wrote the Institutes for Castor before 426 and the Conferences in three parts, Part II (to Honoratus and Eucherius) not later than 426; d. c. 435

names.name: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

voices.hedge: Cassian never mentions Martin, and no surviving story shows a Gallic monk actually keeping the Egyptian program he wrote down. By his own complaint, no one in his own monasteries kept it even for a year.
voices.text: Cassian lived for years among the monks of Egypt before founding two communities of his own at Marseilles. He wrote down what he had learned there, refusing on principle to tell any tale of wonders or signs. He passed on Egypt's own program: purity of heart as the goal, discretion as the guide, and eight faults for a monk to fight in order. He also passed on an unresolved question, one he did not shy from: how much of a monk's progress is God's own gift, and how much is his own effort.

dates.display: founded the community on the island of Lerins c. 400-410 (410 on the surviving volume's editorial introduction); addressed by Cassian as a brother presiding over a large monastery, then as a bishop - the see identified as Arles, from 426, only by the editorial apparatus; d. c. 429/430, the year his disciple and successor Hilary preached his life

names.name: Honoratus, the founder of the island
Honoratus of Lerins, later bishop of Arles (d. c. 429/430)

voices.hedge: The only story told of Honoratus comes from a funeral sermon preached by his own disciple, read today only in rough, hard-to-read Latin. What survives can tell how he arrived on the island and how he left it - nothing of what happened in between.
voices.text: Honoratus went alone to an island so overrun with snakes that no one else would live there, and built a community in a place made for no life at all. He wanted nothing more than to stay a monk. The office of bishop found him anyway, and he ended his life leading the church at Arles instead of the island he founded.

dates.display: writing c. 397 (the Life; Letter III within months of Martin's death) to c. 404-406 (the Dialogues); an Aquitanian 'of an illustrious family' who visited Martin at Tours; birth and death years rest only on the modern editors' disagreeing endnotes and are not asserted

voices.hedge: Nearly everything this world knows about its own northern half passes through this one author's hand. He was not a neutral reporter - he loved Martin and wrote to make readers admire him. Every surviving claim about Tours carries that single-author risk.
voices.text: Sulpitius Severus was rich and well-educated. He gave up his own career to follow Martin. He wrote Martin's Life while Martin was still alive. He says plainly that he was never there for any of the events in it. His real sources were Martin's own household, and sometimes Martin himself.

tile.text: Between about 360 and 450 CE, two households in Roman Gaul lived out one shared idea in different ways: a monk does not stop being a monk just because the Church makes him a bishop. In the Loire valley, a soldier named Martin left the army to serve Christ instead. He gathered followers in the woods near Tours, and the townspeople later seized him and made him their bishop. He never gave up his monk's life. Two generations later, on an island called Lérins off the Mediterranean coast, and in the nearby city of Marseilles, other monks built communities of their own. One of them, John Cassian, had lived among the monks of Egypt. He wrote down what he learned there and adapted it for a colder land and a different church. Another, Vincent, wrote a short rule for telling true growth in the faith from a corruption dressed up as one. Running through both households was one argument, never fully settled: how much of a monk's progress is God's own gift, and how much is his own effort. The two households never had any contact with each other that the surviving evidence can show. The story closes around 450, before that argument hardened into fixed camps.
